domain: Legal History / Intellectual Property / Institutional Economics
topic_summary: Analysis of the Statute of Anne (1710) as a contested kernel in intellectual property law. The statute simultaneously introduced copyright as a conceptual category ('became thinkable') and reallocated institutional rights from the Stationers' Company to authors ('first held'). The kernel contest examines whether these are two readings of one commitment or a spurious synchronic/diachronic cut.

key_entities: Statute of Anne (1710 copyright law establishing limited-term author rights)
Stationers' Company (pre-1710 guild monopoly over printing/publishing)
Parliament/Drafting Committee (legislative authority enacting the statute)
Authors (Daniel Defoe et al.; nominal beneficiaries of the statute)
key_tensions: Property right vs regulatory incentive (preamble shift from 'Securing Property' to 'Encouragement of Learning')
Author rights vs publisher control (statutory beneficiary vs practical beneficiary)
Limited term vs perpetual common law right (statute vs Stationers' subsequent litigation)
Conceptual novelty vs institutional reallocation (new legal category vs power transfer)
Synchronic meaning vs diachronic change (what the statute meant vs what it did)
key_mechanisms: Copyright term structure (21 years existing works, 14+14 years new works)
Manuscript purchase + copyright assignment (publishers buying both text and legal right)
Public domain creation (works entering common pool after term expiration)
key_absences: Definition of 'copy,' 'property,' 'author' in statutory text (drafting ambiguity)
Enforcement mechanism for author rights against publishers (practical power asymmetry)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The Statute of Anne as the founding text establishing copyright as a legal category—a stabilized reference point for what intellectual property is and who holds it
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Parliamentary legislative authority grounded in the statute's text; subsequent judicial interpretation in the copyright wars (1731+) claiming either statutory creation or common law perpetuity

readings.commitment: The statute created a new conceptual space—copyright as a limited regulatory tool for learning, not perpetual property
readings.authority_grounding: Textualist/originalist: the preamble shift from 'Securing Property' to 'Encouragement of Learning' marks the conceptual break
readings.expected_structural_delta: IP 'became thinkable' as a distinct legal category; the space gained a point; beneficiary is public learning; victim is perpetual monopoly

readings.commitment: The statute reallocated existing rights from the Stationers' Company to authors, changing who occupied the institutional space
readings.authority_grounding: Institutional/materialist: the practical effect was power transfer; publishers immediately bought copyrights from authors, perpetuating monopoly
readings.expected_structural_delta: IP 'first held' by a new class; the occupied set changed; beneficiary is publishers (via assignment); victim is Stationers' monopoly

readings.commitment: The statute is a single event with two inseparable dimensions—conceptual and institutional change occurred simultaneously and cannot be disentangled
readings.authority_grounding: Holistic/pragmatist: the synchronic/diachronic distinction is a spurious cut; the copyright wars reveal the statute never resolved the tension
readings.expected_structural_delta: IP is both 'became thinkable' and 'first held' in one act; no clean separation; beneficiary is ambiguous (authors nominal, publishers practical); victim is conceptual clarity

axiom_contradictions.basis: One reading holds that the statute's primary achievement was creating a new legal category (conceptual novelty as the irreducible change); the other holds that the primary achievement was reallocating power (institutional transfer as the irreducible change). No single framework can hold both as the fundamental event—one must be derivative of the other or they collapse into the entangled reading.

omegas.description: Is this a genuine contested kernel or a spurious cut? If the entangled_event_reading is correct, the kernel structure itself forces an artificial separation. The copyright wars (1731+) suggest the statute never resolved the tension, supporting entanglement. But if readings 1 and 2 are genuinely independent (one could occur without the other), the kernel is real.
omegas.source: §1.3-K kernel/not-kernel decision; user's M4/M5 collapse flag

omegas.description: Were the undefined terms ('copy,' 'property,' 'author') a drafting failure or a deliberate snare? If deliberate, publishers are beneficiaries of intentional ambiguity. If failure, the snare is emergent. Evidence: Stationers' lobbying success suggests intentional vagueness to preserve flexibility.
omegas.source: Deferred axis drafting_ambiguity_extraction; Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan)

omegas.description: Did authors have genuine agency in the institutional reallocation, or were they nominal beneficiaries in a publisher-controlled system? The manuscript+copyright purchase pattern suggests the latter, but Defoe's advocacy suggests some authors understood the stakes. Affects whether institutional_reallocation_reading's victim is authors or Stationers.
omegas.source: Extraction tension: author rights vs publisher control; institutional_reallocation_reading beneficiary ambiguity

omegas.description: Did copyright exist in common law before the statute (Stationers' claim) or was it created by the statute (textualist claim)? This is the copyright wars' central question. If common law perpetuity is valid, the statute is institutional reallocation only. If not, the statute is conceptual emergence. Unresolved in the research context.
omegas.source: Extraction tension: limited vs perpetual rights; conceptual_emergence vs institutional_reallocation axiom contradiction
